findings.title: Profile-as-data cannot express four of the five archetypes the document claims it covers
findings.description: "All behavioral variation comes from parameterized profiles, not from archetype-specific code paths. Adding a new species or creature means defining a new profile, not writing new simulation logic" and "The same force-accumulation loop handles all archetypes" (line 79) are false for the archetypes described in `Envisioned State`: herding needs "leadership tendency (experienced individuals)" — `AgentState` (100-slice, `src/migratory/engine/state.py`) has only positions, velocities, accelerations, profile_indices, no age/experience/leader field; pack hunting needs "convergence-on-target behavior" and target selection, which is a decision, explicitly forbidden by the `Forces, not decisions` principle; territorial needs "home-range attraction", requiring a per-agent home center that does not exist; swarm "respond to environmental stigmergy (reinforced paths)", which requires *writing* markers while `Architectural Principles` mandates a read-only environment interface. `Technical Considerations#Inter-archetype interactions` admits "Profile-to-profile interaction rules add a combinatorial dimension to the parameter space" but provides no place for an interaction matrix in the flat scalar `BehavioralProfile` dataclass or in the `BulkForce` signature. Realizing these archetypes requires new state arrays, new force code, a target-selection mechanism, and a writable environment — i.e., exactly the archetype-specific code paths the design forbids. This is a rearchitecture, not a tuning exercise.

findings.title: The mandated neighbor interface makes the vectorized, GPU-ready hot loop impossible and the 10K-agent goal unreachable
findings.description: `Design Goals` requires "tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process" and "The hot loop must be structured for vectorized computation over arrays of agent state, not object-by-object iteration"; the GPU section requires "bulk array-in/array-out operations with no Python-level per-agent branching, no dynamic allocation, and no callbacks into Python". The interface the document actually mandates (subset-evaluable tick + per-agent `query_radius`) resolves in `src/migratory/engine/tick.py` into `for idx in eval_indices: neighbors = spatial.query_radius(...)`, where `BruteForceQuery.query_radius` recomputes `self._positions - position` plus `np.linalg.norm` over all N agents per call — O(n²) with an N×2 temporary allocation per agent. Each of the three forces in `src/migratory/engine/flocking.py` then runs *another* `for ... enumerate(eval_indices)` loop and allocates `np.zeros((n, 2))`. So there are four Python-level per-agent passes per tick with per-agent allocation: precisely the object-by-object iteration and dynamic allocation the doc forbids. At 10K agents/20Hz this is ~100M distance evaluations per tick plus ~40K Python iterations, far beyond the 50ms budget in 300-arch. Furthermore `BulkForce` passes `profiles: list[BehavioralProfile]` (Python dataclasses) and ragged `neighbor_lists: list[NDArray]` — neither is a device array, so "structurally identical to a GPU compute dispatch" is wrong. Slice 101 explicitly accepted the Python loop for "hundreds to low thousands", and slice 105 only swaps the spatial index, leaving the three per-agent force loops intact.

findings.title: The system-level interface is described three incompatible ways and none matches the tick contract
findings.description: `Envisioned State` step 5 says "Returns the updated state array", line 70 says "feed in state, get back state. No setup, no teardown, no mocks" and "The engine is stateless between ticks", and line 81 claims a "narrow interface: tick the simulation forward, query agent state, register/remove agents". The implemented `tick()` (`src/migratory/engine/tick.py`, slice 100 "Output: AgentState mutated in place", slice 303 "state mutated in place") returns `None` and mutates the caller's `AgentState` in place. It needs six arguments including a `SpatialQuery` instance, `profiles`, and `forces` — that is setup — and `BruteForceQuery._positions` plus `SimulationManager._spatial/_forces/_profiles/_dt` are state retained between ticks, so "stateless" is false. There is no "query agent state" API, and register/remove is explicitly the server's job (300-arch: "Entity management is centralized in the server ... the behavior engine ... does not manage the entity lifecycle itself"; 300-slices 302 `EntityManager.spawn_entity/remove_entity`). Most consequentially, 300-arch's `Tick as transaction` principle and its step 4 "State commit — Apply the updated entity state as the new canonical state" cannot be honored: with in-place mutation the canonical state is live during computation, so a force that raises leaves partially integrated positions with no rollback path. The concept's "keep the tick function pure" is likewise violated. This ambiguity spans three documents and governs replay/distribution.

findings.title: The subset contract promises a mask form that the interface cannot accept, and misstates implementation status
findings.description: `Architectural Principles` says the tick "accepts an agent subset (index array or mask)" (repeated at line 64). The actual contract is `active_indices: NDArray[np.intp] | None` (slice 100 says "index array" only). A boolean mask silently breaks: `tick()` iterates `for idx in eval_indices` and `flocking.py` iterates `for agent_idx in eval_indices`, so entries become `True`/`False` and `profiles[state.profile_indices[True]]` indexes nonsense; `integrate()` uses `velocities[idx] += ...`, where a mask has different semantics and duplicate indices are silently under-applied by NumPy's fancy-index buffering. No validation contract exists for out-of-range or duplicate subsets, violating the project rule against silent fallbacks. The same principle claims "The initial implementation evaluates all agents" — false: slice 100 implemented and tested subset evaluation (`TestSubsetEvaluation`), while slice 303 explicitly excludes multi-resolution use. A caller following the document and passing a mask gets silently wrong simulation results.

findings.title: Partial-agent ticking has no per-agent timestep or last-evaluated state, so the "foundation for multi-resolution" does not work
findings.description: `Multi-resolution simulation and aggregation` states the tick "must accept partial agent subsets" so the world server can do "variable-rate ticking (some agents evaluated every tick, others at 1/4 or 1/16 rate)". But `tick()` takes one scalar `dt` and applies it uniformly (`integrate(positions, velocities, total_forces, dt, ...)`). An agent evaluated at 1/4 rate must integrate over four ticks of elapsed time; with a single-tick `dt` it travels a quarter the distance of its full-rate neighbors, so heterogeneous subsets produce different dynamics from the same profile — breaking `Tick determinism` and archetype fidelity. There is no per-agent dt, no accumulator of ticks since last evaluation, and no interpolation contract; since the doc declares the engine "stateless between ticks", the caller must own that state, but `tick()` has no parameter to receive it. 300-arch's "interpolated positions between evaluations" addresses rendering, not force/integration error. Likewise `Envisioned State` step 2 lets inactive agents be neighbors, but `AlignmentForce` reads their velocities, which are stale by 4–16 ticks — no policy for stale-velocity handling exists. The advertised extension point cannot support the stated future work without rearchitecting the tick signature and state ownership.

findings.title: The SpatialQuery and neighbor-list shapes block every replacement the document promises, and aggregates cannot be expressed at all
findings.description: "the interface must support replacement with grid, KD-tree, or GPU-accelerated alternatives without changing the engine" and `Technical Considerations` adds "replaced without touching the force computation code". The defined protocol (`src/migratory/spatial/interface.py`, slice 100) is `build(positions)` + one `query_radius(position, radius)` call per active agent returning `NDArray[np.intp]`. A spatial hash needs world bounds/cell size with no parameter available — slice 303 claims the query is "initialized with world bounds from server config" but `BruteForceQuery()` takes no arguments. SciPy `cKDTree.query_ball_point` and any CuPy kernel are batched over query points; one dispatch per agent is the wrong granularity. So a genuine replacement requires changing `SpatialQuery`, `tick()`, *and* `BulkForce`, because every force consumes the ragged `list[NDArray[np.intp]]` — the spatial strategy is leaked into all force code. Aggregates are worse: line 97 says "the world server would present [them] through the same neighbor query interface", yet an aggregate has center of mass, heading, dispersion, and count, while `query_radius` returns only integer indices into `state.positions` and `CohesionForce`/`AlignmentForce` index `state.positions[neighbors]` and `state.velocities[neighbors]`. There is no type tag, no dispersion/count channel, and no way to distinguish an aggregate from an individual. Ownership is circular too: 100-slices (108) "Aggregation Interface Support" depends on "World Server multi-resolution implementation", while 300-slices lists "Multi-Resolution Entity Simulation" as Future Work depending on (303) — both sides defer the contract this doc says must exist "from the start".

findings.title: The "environment as input surface" interface is never defined, and read-only is contradicted by stigmergy and by the server's post-tick writes
findings.description: Step 1 says the engine "Receives the current agent state array, environmental context", step 3 evaluates forces "against its local neighborhood and environment", and `Architectural Principles` promises "terrain elevation, resource locations, threat zones, seasonal parameters ... through a read-only interface". No such interface is specified anywhere: no type, no method names, no data shapes, no statement of whether it is per-agent bulk data or per-tick scalar context. `tick()` (`src/migratory/engine/tick.py`) has no environment parameter, and there are zero environment/bounds references anywhere under `src/migratory`. Since `Overview` explicitly puts "the interfaces these present to the rest of the system" in scope, this is a missing load-bearing interface rather than deferred detail. It is also self-contradictory: line 76 requires swarm agents to use "environmental stigmergy (reinforced paths)", which needs marker *deposits*, and 300-slices slice 304 says "Handle post-tick environment writes (e.g., stigmergic trail deposits)" and "Pass environment context to `SimulationManager` and `engine.tick()`" — a write path and a parameter that do not exist. Seasonal migration, a concept-level headline, likewise has no route into force evaluation. The named provider (initiative 500 Environment Layer) is `not_started` in `001-initiative-plan.migratory.md` and depends on 300, so "handled by X" points at nothing today.

findings.title: Load-bearing representations are left implicit: dimensionality, precision, world bounds, and RNG seed
findings.description: `Array layout for vectorized computation` says SoA "needs validation" and `State serialization boundary` says "the engine should define its internal precision" — neither decision is made, yet both are load-bearing. The implementation is `DIMS = 2` (`src/migratory/__init__.py`) with float64 arrays, while `WorldBoundsConfig(width, height)` and `SpawnAreaConfig(x,y)` in `src/migratory_server/config.py` are 2D and all three flocking forces hardcode `np.zeros((n, 2))`. So `Clean boundaries` — "Internal representation choices ... are hidden behind these interfaces and replaceable without affecting consumers" — is false; a 3D world (implied by the Three.js terrain prototype and "terrain elevation") forces changes to config schema, `EntityManager`, every force, spatial queries, and the wire protocol. There is no world-boundary policy at all: `config/default.yaml` defines 1000×1000 bounds and slice 302 validates spawn areas, but `tick()` integrates unbounded, so agents leave the finite world; 300-arch lists "boundary-driven (entities leaving world bounds)" as a future lifecycle event source with no wrap/clamp/reflect rule — which also undermines "regions must agree on simulation results from shared boundary state". Finally, determinism/replay has no seed ownership: slice 302's `spawn_population` uses unseeded `np.random.default_rng()` (its slice notes "non-deterministic"), `SimulationConfig` has no seed, yet 300-arch's replay strategy assumes "logging only the initial state plus any non-deterministic inputs is sufficient". The initial state is non-deterministic and unseeded, and no reduction-order rule for `np.mean` over neighbors is given for cross-region agreement.

findings.title: No failure, validation, or numerical-stability strategy exists anywhere in the design
findings.description: This is cross-cutting: I read every section of the document (`Overview`, `Design Goals`, `Architectural Principles`, `Current State`, `Envisioned State`, `Technical Considerations`, `Anticipated Slices`, `Related Work`) and none specifies how any engine failure is detected, reported, or recovered. Concrete gaps: `SeparationForce` in `src/migratory/engine/flocking.py` computes `diff / dist**2` after self-exclusion, so two distinct co-located agents give `dist = 0` → `inf`/`NaN`, which propagates through `total_forces` into positions and velocities permanently with no NaN guard; there is no validation policy for NaN/inf profile weights, out-of-range `profile_indices`, or empty/invalid `active_indices` (see the mask/duplicate problem above); no contract for what happens if `spatial.build()` or a `BulkForce` raises mid-tick — combined with in-place mutation, that commits partially updated canonical state with no rollback (contradicting 300-arch's `Tick as transaction` and the project convention "Never use silent fallback values. Fail explicitly with errors"). `Tick rate and integration stability` names Euler energy drift and suggests Verlet but never picks a rule, force clamp, or overflow policy. The document's only treatment of errors is delegating tick *timing* overruns to 300-arch; computational failure modes are entirely assumed away.

findings.title: The per-agent Python loop defeats the asyncio server model and the GIL-based offload upgrade path
findings.description: The stack is Python 3.12 + NumPy + asyncio (concept `Initial Technical Direction`; `pyproject.toml`). `Overview` delegates "timing, scheduling, asyncio yielding" to 300-arch, whose coexistence plan is "run the tick synchronously, then yield to the async event loop for I/O between ticks ... If tick computation grows to consume the full budget, offloading the tick to a thread or process (NumPy releases the GIL) becomes the upgrade path". That plan is only valid if the tick really is vectorized C-level NumPy. The engine design here dictates a Python-level per-agent loop for neighbor queries and force accumulation (see the FAIL finding on the hot loop), which holds the GIL for the entire tick; `SimulationManager.step()` in slice 303 is synchronous with no `await` inside, so `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on overrun cannot run until the tick finishes. At the 10K–50K tier, WebSocket I/O (slice 305) is starved for full tick durations and thread offload yields no parallelism. This is a sync/async mismatch created by the engine's interface choices, and the document never reconciles it with the host process it explicitly targets. Relatedly, the promised "KD-tree" replacement would need SciPy (mentioned in the concept), but `pyproject.toml` declares only `numpy` and `pyyaml` — no dependency decision is recorded.

findings.title: Related Work points to a nonexistent world-server architecture document, and the document disagrees with itself about its number
findings.description: Line 122 links `[200-arch.world-server-foundation.md](200-arch.world-server-foundation.md)`. No such file exists in `project-documents/user/architecture/`; the actual document is `300-arch.worldserver-foundation.md`, and line 21 (`Overview`) correctly calls it "300-arch". `100-slices.behavior-engine.md` Notes repeats the same dead `200-arch` link. The 300-arch document in turn links to `../project-guides/001-concept.migratory.md`, which also does not exist (the concept is `000-concept.migratory.md`), so the two architecture documents cannot be navigated to each other or to their shared concept. This is not cosmetic: the scaling tiers, aggregation strategy, and "tick as transaction" assumptions cited throughout this document are sourced from the document it fails to identify correctly, and the numeric mismatch (`200-arch` vs `300-arch` vs the initiative plan's `300` band) makes the dependency reference ambiguous.

findings.title: Swarm intelligence and seasonal migration — scope the initiative plan assigns to this architecture — are dropped from the slice structure
findings.description: `001-initiative-plan.migratory.md` initiative (100) assigns the Behavior Engine "all behavioral archetypes (flocking, herding, predator-prey, territorial, swarm intelligence)" and "spatial indexing"; the concept's `User-Provided Concept` makes "seasonal cycles driving migration patterns" a headline requirement. `Design Goals` here still promises "visually and statistically distinguishable movement patterns for each behavioral archetype (... swarm intelligence)". But `Anticipated Slices` lists seven slices with no swarm intelligence and no migration/seasonal movement, and `100-slices.behavior-engine.md` pushes both into `Future Work` — (106) Swarm Intelligence and (107) Migration and Seasonal Movement — gated on the Environment Layer initiative, which the initiative plan marks `not_started` and dependent on 300. Two of five named archetypes plus the concept's headline long-term behavior therefore have neither a slice nor an interface slot, while the architecture simultaneously claims to reserve interface slots "from the start" for the much more speculative aggregation and GPU work. The architecture must either reserve the environment/marker and seasonal-parameter interfaces it needs, or explicitly renegotiate the scope assigned by the plan instead of quietly deferring it.

findings.title: The architecture is overweight for a first computational core: several mechanisms have no consumer and constrain the implementation into a non-vectorizable shape
findings.description: Initiative 100's near-term deliverable (per `100-slices.behavior-engine.md` slices 100–105) is a brute-force tick plus four force types. Against that, the document specifies: subset-evaluable tick (slice 303 explicitly excludes multi-resolution; the world server's use is Future Work), aggregate-neighbor support (100-slices 108 Future Work, world-server side also Future Work), GPU no-allocation/no-Python-branch constraints (initiative 620 is "deliberately deferred ... it need not be designed proactively"), a dual `Force`/`BulkForce` protocol where the per-agent `Force` is exercised only by the test placeholder `ConstantDriftSingle`, and two subset encodings where only one exists. The naive `BruteForceQuery` is what actually runs and cannot reach the 10K tier, so this machinery buys nothing now while forcing the ragged, per-agent shape that makes the vectorization and GPU goals impossible. It is also an upward dependency: the foundation's interface is derived from a consumer's deferred roadmap. Per the project convention "Always resist adding complexity. Ensure it is truly necessary", cut: the mask form, the per-agent `Force` protocol, and the aggregate/GPU constraints from the v1 contract; keep only `active_indices` (index array), `profiles`, `dt`, `forces`, and replace per-agent `query_radius` with a single batched bulk neighbor query that a spatial hash *and* a later GPU path can implement. Move the 4M+/multi-GPU and aggregation discussion to initiative 620. This cuts speculative mechanism, not the archetypes the plan assigns (which the preceding finding asks to restore).

findings.title: "Clean boundaries" is false: the server writes engine arrays directly, the profile schema is an unversioned shared contract, and the server is currently broken by it
findings.description: `Clean boundaries` claims "Internal representation choices (array layout, spatial index strategy) are hidden behind these interfaces and replaceable without affecting consumers", and `Profile as data` claims profiles "can be serialized, loaded from configuration, and swapped at runtime". In `src/migratory_server/entities.py`, `EntityManager` writes `AgentState.positions/velocities/accelerations/profile_indices` directly with `np.concatenate`, and 300-arch requires the server to serialize those raw buffers — layout is a shared contract, not hidden. `BehavioralProfile` is one mutable dataclass with all six scalar fields required, shared by both packages, with no versioning, codec, or serialization format; slice 101 added four required fields and every consumer broke. Concretely: `build_profiles()` in `src/migratory_server/simulation.py` still constructs `BehavioralProfile(max_speed=..., query_radius=...)`, so `Server.run()` → `build_profiles()` raises `TypeError: missing 4 required positional arguments` against the shipped `config/default.yaml`; `ProfileConfig` in `config.py` has only three fields and `tests/test_simulation.py::TestBuildProfiles` calls that same helper, contradicting slice 303's "202 tests pass" and its promise that "Slice 101 will extend `ProfileConfig` with force weights". Runtime swap is likewise absent: `SimulationManager._profiles` and `EntityManager._profile_list` are built once at startup and `profile_indices` are baked into `AgentState`; slice 303 excludes "Dynamic profile changes at runtime". Finally, `State serialization boundary` says the format "should either be directly serializable (e.g., raw Float32 buffers) or have a zero-copy serialization path" and then proposes a float64→Float32 "efficient conversion path" — a conversion is by definition not zero-copy. The boundary needs a versioned profile schema with a config codec, or a stable key/value parameter mapping, plus an explicit statement of which arrays consumers may touch.
